https://www.politico.eu/article/kaja-kal.text: An EU-wide ban on trade with illegal Israeli settlements would be a “principled stance” to take for the bloc, the EU’s top diplomat Kaja Kallas said, comparing illegal settlements in the West Bank to Russia’s occupation of Crimea. “If we take the example when Crimea was occupied, then it was very clear, it’s illegal, we don’t recognize this, which means that we stop the trade with any products that come from Crimea,” Kallas said in an interview with the Irish Times published Friday. “We should have the same principled stance — you know this is illegal, everybody agrees — so we should stop trading with Occupied Territories.” Israel’s mission to the EU and NATO described the comments as “deeply unfortunate.” Advertisement Advertisement “Especially today, on the eve of the Jewish New Year, it is hard to believe that [she] would draw a direct parallel between The Western wall and the Jewish Quarter in Jerusalem and the situation in Crimea, regardless of her personal worldview,” the mission said. The EU foreign policy chief has long backed a push from several member countries to pressure the European Commission to ban trade with territories illegally occupied by Israel — an issue that divides capitals and has become a flashpoint in the rift between Kallas and the Commission’s president, Ursula von der Leyen. Kallas’ backing has so far failed to force the Commission’s hand . In July, only a minority of EU foreign ministers called on the Commission to bring specific measures for member countries to vote on. While a handful of countries including the Netherlands, Belgium and Sweden have pushed for bloc-wide restrictions, the Czech Republic has vowed to oppose any new sanctions — withholding the unanimity required among EU capitals. But the debate was reignited Tuesday when eight EU countries, including France, Spain and Ireland, joined the U.K. and Canada in a pledge to impose trade sanctions on Israeli settlements. “All EU Member States agree that Israeli settlements in the West Bank are illegal under international law,” Kallas said after the announcement . “The Israeli Government’s settlement expansions in the West Bank are undermining the prospects for a viable two-State solution.” Kallas’ positions have previously drawn the ire of Israeli officials. Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Sa’ar vowed to “sever all contact” with the EU’s top diplomat in June, after reports that she had compared Israel’s treatment of Palestinians to apartheid-era South Africa. https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text: ‘Friedrich Merz is already looking like a lame duck leader.’ Photograph: Filip Singer/EPA View image in fullscreen ‘Friedrich Merz is already looking like a lame duck leader.’ Photograph: Filip Singer/EPA Opinion Germany The Guardian view on Friedrich Merz: Germany’s chancellor must change course to halt the rise of the AfD Editorial A failure to address widespread economic insecurity, and a crisis in living standards, is allowing the far right the harness a growing protest vote Mon 21 Sep 2026 13.34 EDT Last modified on Mon 21 Sep 2026 14.01 EDT Share A fter less than a year and a half in office, Germany’s beleaguered chancellor, Friedrich Merz, is already looking like a lame duck leader. Anticipating dire results in two state elections which were held on Sunday, Mr Merz cancelled a planned speech at this week’s United Nations general assembly in order to plot an emergency response. A night of extraordinary humiliation for his conservative Christian Democratic Union party (CDU) must have confounded even his own low expectations. In the eastern state of Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, the far-right Alternative für Deutschland party (AfD) won its second regional election this month with 38% of the vote. The CDU meanwhile recorded its worst result since the second world war, failing even to meet the 5% threshold for representation in the state parliament. Mr Merz took over the leadership of the CDU promising to see off the threat of the AfD. Instead it has ascended to a menacing and unprecedented position of electoral strength, and enjoys a comfortable lead in national polls. View image in fullscreen Elif Eralp of the Left party. Photograph: Clemens Bilan/EPA In the other regional contest, the CDU ceded control of the mayoralty in Berlin and finished second behind the radical Left party, which campaigned on a platform to address the capital’s soaring housing crisis . These were seminal reverses, but Mr Merz shows no sign of learning the lessons from either defeat. Defiantly dismissing speculation over his future, he insisted that his coalition government was “determined to live up to the historic responsibilities our country is facing”. Without a change of political direction that seems improbable. Suffering from depopulation and persistent inequalities relative to the west, Germany’s eastern regions have been particularly vulnerable to the rise of one of Europe’s most extreme far-right movements. But as the continent’s powerhouse economy struggles with Chinese competition, US protectionism, and a cost of living crisis , there is nationwide disillusionment with the chancellor’s abrasive style and “tough love” prescriptions. Mr Merz’s personal poll ratings hover at a record low of around 13%. Doubling down on a programme which includes raising the retirement age, cutting health insurance benefits, and making it much more difficult to claim sick leave, is hardly likely to turn those numbers around. The Social Democratic party (SPD), as the junior coalition partner, has attempted to act as a partial brake on the chancellor’s pro-austerity instincts. But as one of its despairing MPs acidly observed of Mr Merz: “He constantly asks people to work more, while tens of thousands of jobs are currently being cut in German industry!” The constitutional obstacles to removing a chancellor – and the reality that neither the CDU nor the SPD want a new election given the state of their respective polling – mean that Mr Merz is likely to stay in post. But if the government’s fortunes are to revive, a radical rethink is required. The chancellor’s unsuccessful strategy for spiking the AfD’s guns has been to ape its draconian positions on immigration. But it is the failure to address a crisis in living standards and widespread economic insecurity which allows the far right to channel a growing protest vote. That is deeply worrying. On Monday, Mr Merz emphasised that Germany’s “democratic future” must be defended. He was right to emphasise how much is at stake. But it is becoming increasingly and alarmingly clear how ill-suited he is for that task. Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? https://spacedaily.com/k-the-stalactites.text: A show cave is what speleologists call any cave that has been developed for public tourism. There are around a thousand of them worldwide. Some are hundreds of thousands of years old and are famous for their prehistoric art. Others are famous for their vast subterranean chambers hung with stalactites the size of freight trains. Almost all of them are, in strict geological terms, extremely stable microclimatic environments where the temperature holds steady within a fraction of a degree year-round, the humidity sits close to saturation, and the CO2 concentration reflects the slow natural exchange between the underlying karst rock and the atmosphere above. That stability is what allowed the formations inside to grow undisturbed over hundreds of thousands of years in the first place. It is also what makes the caves extraordinarily sensitive to any change in the air composition once the public start walking through them in significant numbers. The problem is that people breathe. And when a group of forty tourists walks into a small underground chamber and stands there for fifteen minutes while a guide explains what they’re looking at, the collective exhalation of those forty people releases enough warm humid CO2-saturated air into the chamber to shift the entire local atmosphere in ways that the stalactites, quite literally, cannot survive if it happens often enough. How the chemistry actually works The mechanism is straightforward once you follow it through. Every exhaled human breath contains roughly one hundred times more CO2 than ambient outside air, along with a substantial load of water vapour at body temperature. When that breath enters a cave whose walls are cooler than the exhaled air, the water vapour immediately condenses onto the nearest cool surface, which is usually the surface of whatever calcite formation the tourists have gathered to look at. The condensed water, having formed from air that was rich in CO2, is now itself rich in dissolved CO2. Rich-in-CO2 water is acidic. Specifically it’s a weak solution of carbonic acid. And carbonic acid, when it comes into contact with calcium carbonate, which is what stalactites and stalagmites are made of, dissolves it. The formation loses a microscopic layer of surface calcite every time the process happens. If learning about our world fascinates you, check out this video on the silent fire burning under the Arctic: What changed in the universe since you were born? Six sourced measurements. No predictions. No astrology. According to a 2024 peer-reviewed paper in Nature’s Scientific Reports by researchers at the Universidad de Alicante, IAA-CSIC, and CNRS France, led by Marina Sáez and coordinated by Sylvain Mangiarotti and Sergio Sánchez-Moral , the effect at Altamira Cave in Cantabria, Spain, was measured and quantified across decades of continuous instrumentation. Altamira, which was open to public tourism from 1917 through most of the twentieth century, reached CO2 concentrations of nearly 20,000 parts per million during the peak visitor era of the 1970s, when 174,613 people were passing through the cave in a single year. The natural background concentration in the region’s outside atmosphere was around 400 ppm. The concentration inside the cave was, at various moments during the 1970s, up to fifty times that. And on the calculation of a separate 1999 paper by Sánchez-Moral and colleagues, the corrosion rate on the cave’s walls during that period was enhanced by a factor of 78 compared to what would have occurred through natural processes alone. Altamira closed to the public in 1977 after the effects became undeniable. It reopened briefly with restricted numbers between 1982 and 2002. It closed again in 2002 after biologists discovered actively growing communities of green algae, fungi, and bacteria on the walls, all of which were feeding on the microscopic quantities of skin flakes, hair fibres, and clothing lint that visitors had been shedding into the cave environment over the previous decades. The paintings themselves, which are among the most significant works of Paleolithic art anywhere in the world, are still being conserved. Only a small number of researchers now enter the cave. Everybody else visits a replica built above ground. What’s happening in the caves still open to the public The Altamira story is not unique. Lascaux in France, which is the other most famous Paleolithic art site in Europe, closed in 1963 for essentially the same reasons and has never reopened to the public. Chauvet Cave, which was discovered in southern France in 1994 and contains even older paintings than Lascaux, has never been open to the public at all, on the direct recommendation of the archaeologists who found it. Both sites now offer public tours of underground replicas built nearby with painstaking accuracy. Neither of the originals is likely ever to be visited by non-specialists again. Meanwhile, the show caves that are still open to the public are dealing with the same chemistry at different scales. According to a 2021 peer-reviewed study in the journal Sustainability by Silviu Constantin and colleagues at Romania’s Emil Racoviță Institute of Speleology, monitoring four Romanian show caves over two years of continuous CO2 measurements , the Urșilor Cave in the Apuseni Mountains, which attracts more than 120,000 visitors annually, was found to have CO2 concentrations exceeding 14,000 ppm during peak summer months when up to 200 tourists were entering per hour. Point measurements taken with portable instruments during August 2016 found CO2 levels that briefly crossed the safety threshold for occupational exposure. The recovery of the cave microclimate back to normal levels was measured at approximately two weeks, meaning that during high tourist season the cave never actually returned to its natural state at all. It was in a state of continuous chemical perturbation from June through September. The Constantin team also documented that the drip water inside the cave had become chemically aggressive to calcite, meaning that the very water dripping onto the formations that visitors were paying to see was now, because of the elevated CO2 environment the visitors themselves were producing, in the process of dissolving those formations rather than adding to them. In other words, the cave was no longer growing. It was corroding. And the visitors were the reason. The additional complications include what speleologists call lampenflora, meaning the algae, mosses, ferns, and microbial communities that grow on cave walls in the constant illumination of the electric lights installed for the tourists. Lampenflora physically covers the calcite surfaces, blocks the natural light-sensitive processes, and produces its own weak organic acids as it grows, contributing further to the corrosion of the underlying rock. It has proven remarkably difficult to eliminate once it establishes itself. Switching to LED lighting reduces the effect but does not remove it. Chemical treatments select for resistant strains within a few generations of the microbes involved. The most reliable eradication method is total darkness for extended periods, which is exactly what a working show cave cannot provide. The current international consensus among cave conservation specialists is essentially that the paradox is real and mostly unresolvable. The formations people want to see took hundreds of thousands of years to grow. The corrosion caused by people wanting to see them happens on human timescales, measured in decades rather than geological eras. Every extended visit shortens the future viewing life of the specific chamber being visited. Some caves have responded by drastically limiting visitor numbers, replacing lighting systems, banning group photography with flash, and building airlocks at every entrance to slow the exchange of atmospheres. Others have gone the Altamira route and closed the original site entirely in favour of a purpose-built replica above ground. And the tourists who come specifically because they want to stand inside the actual cave, breathing the actual air, looking at the actual formations, are, in the strict physical sense, the reason those formations may not be there for the tourists who come after them. Photograph: Abdul Saboor/Reuters View image in fullscreen The Marianne statue wears a yellow vest in the Place de la République in Paris after riots at the weekend. Photograph: Abdul Saboor/Reuters France France to deploy 70,000 police on Saturday to prevent civil unrest Security forces to include elite units usually used for counter-terrorism after worst street violence in years Europe live – latest updates Jon Henley in Paris Fri 23 Oct 2026 11.34 EDT First published on Fri 23 Oct 2026 10.31 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google France will deploy about 70,000 police around the country on Saturday as the government seeks to prevent more civil unrest after some of the worst street violence in years erupted on the fringes of cost-of-living protests last weekend. The interior minister, Laurent Nuñez, said on ⁠Friday ⁠the security forces would include elite units usually used for counter-terrorism operations and hostage rescues, adding that there had been social media calls for violence from “ultra-left” groups. “We are not talking about ⁠a peaceful, friendly demonstration,” Nuñez ​told reporters after a meeting of senior ministers and officials chaired by the president, Emmanuel Macron . “We ​are ​ready tomorrow ​to be ‌extremely firm ​and ​not tolerate anything.” Macron and his government are struggling to get on top of a crisis that has caught it off guard six months before presidential elections to choose his successor. The government has admitted it “lost control” over widespread rioting on Saturday. View image in fullscreen A demonstrator reads a book on the street at a protest organised by student collectives and trade unions in Paris on 22 October. Photograph: Abdul Saboor/Reuters Angry lawyers and bewildered defendants: the fallout from fast-tracking French rioting cases Read more Largely peaceful demonstrations were hijacked by groups of determined rioters, degenerating into rampant violence and extensive looting in Paris, Marseille, Lyon and other cities. In Limoges, the town hall was set on fire and partly destroyed. “We will be uncompromising with rioters, looters and all who commit violence,” Nuñez said, adding that besides 10,000 more police, the operation would include water cannon, armoured vehicles, mounted police, helicopters and drones. Demonstrations are expected in several other countries this weekend, triggered by a broader, continent-wide wave of discontent over declining public services, housing affordability, public sector budget cuts and the spiralling cost of living. Protests over related grievances have been called for Saturday in Milan, Rome and Turin in Italy; in Vienna, Austria; and in Madrid, Barcelona and other cities in Spain, as well as in Lisbon and Porto in Portugal, Dublin in Ireland and Tirana in Albania. Historic Limoges city hall collapses after being set ablaze Protests are expected across France on Saturday, although several cities have banned demonstrations or forced them to change their planned routes to protect shops and public buildings, and forecast heavy rain and high winds could dampen turnout. The centres of Lyon and some other large cities will be off-limits to protesters, while authorities in Paris authorised a union march along a limited route in the east of the capital between the Places de la Bastille and Nation that will avoid the city centre. But requests for rallies in Paris organised by France’s main student union, UNEF, and the gilets jaunes movement, whose nationwide protests rocked France in 2018 and which plans 600 small-scale events around France on Saturday, were refused. UNEF said its rallies, which grew from high school protests last month against teacher shortages and dilapidated facilities, would go ahead regardless. Several of the best-known cultural institutions in Paris, including the Louvre, said they would close on Saturday. View image in fullscreen People walk past a closed Monoprix store in Lyon, France, after protests turned violent. Photograph: Lisi Niesner/Reuters Authorities in Marseille had also banned all protests, but announced on Friday that a union-organised demonstration would be allowed on an “exceptional basis”. It will be the only authorised protest in the southern Bouches-du-Rhône department. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to This is Europe The most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environment after newsletter promotion ‘An orchestra being gassed should be an alarm signal’: the musical activists targeted in Paris Read more Unionists and opposition leaders have criticised the government for refusing to allow more rallies on Saturday, a decision being challenged in court in several cities. Marylise Léon of the CFDT union federation accused Macron of an abuse of authority. “It’s ​counterproductive because there is a lot ​of anger and a demand to be considered and to be listened to,” Léon, the CFDT’s general secretary, told TF1 TV. “It’s not for the president to decide who can legitimately protest.” La France Insoumise, the radical left party of Jean-Luc Mélenchon, said the government had “crossed the lines that separate a democracy from an authoritarian and police state”, adding that the bans would only “generate more chaos”. Adding to the tensions, the far-right leader Marine Le Pen, the frontrunner for next spring’s presidential elections, is due to host her National Rally (RN) party congress in Orléans, drawing thousands of supporters – and leftwing, anti-racist opponents. View image in fullscreen French police attending the aftermath of a shooting in Trappes, near Paris, in which one person was killed and four injured. Photograph: Yoan Valat/EPA Nuñez was due to visit the city on Friday to “inspect the security arrangements” at the request of the prime minister’s office. The justice minister, Gérald Darmanin, said 217 people – half of them first-time offenders – had been jailed since Saturday. On Thursday, Macron called for “the utmost severity” against “acts of delinquency”, saying gangs of rioters had been mainly responsible for the looting but the worst violence was caused by “ultra-left” groups seeking to “bring down the republic”. Further stoking disquiet, one person was killed and four others injured – including a 12-year-old girl – in ⁠a shooting in the town of Trappes, west of Paris, on Friday in an attack that police said could have been racially motivated.
